title: Fourier Series
body:
when $f$ converges such that 
$$
f(x) \sim \frac{a_{0}}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left[a_{n}\cos(nx) + b_{b}\sin(nx)\right]
$$
Where
$$
\begin{dcases}
a_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\cos(nx)dx, \quad n=0,1,2,\dots  \\
b_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)dx, \quad n=0,1,2,\dots 
\end{dcases}
$$
---

Pointer added 2026-08-16 during MATH 2200's pass: **this is the other way to write a function as an
infinite sum, and the contrast with [[Taylor Series]] is the useful thing to hold.** A Taylor series
uses powers of $(x-a)$, is built from **derivatives at one point**, and is therefore *local*: it
matches beautifully near $a$ and can fail entirely outside a radius. A Fourier series uses sines and
cosines, is built from **integrals over a whole period**, and is therefore *global*: it sees the
function everywhere at once, which is why it copes with a square wave that is not even
differentiable. The coefficients above are integrals, so they are evaluated with
[[Trigonometric Integrals]] and [[Integration By Parts]] from [[CALCULUS 2]], and the convergence
questions are [[Infinite Series]] questions.

Added 2026-08-16 during MATH 3200's pass: **the physical reason these series exist is separation of
variables.** Solving the [[Heat Equation]] or the [[Wave Equation]] on a bounded interval produces a
family of modes ($\sin(n\pi x/L)$ and friends), and fitting a given initial condition to them is
exactly the expansion above. See [[Partial Differential Equations]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]: the
harmonics of a plucked string are the $n$ of this series, and the coefficients are how loud each one
is.

---

**Where this goes next in the course.** [[Fourier Coefficients]] are the $a_n$ and $b_n$ above and
[[Orthogonal Functions]] is why their integrals work. [[Complex Exponential]] rewrites the whole
series as $\sum c_n e^{inx}$, one coefficient family instead of two. [[Gibbs Phenomenon]] is what
happens at a jump and [[Parseval's Identity]] is the conservation law the coefficients obey. Let
the period go to infinity and the series becomes the [[Fourier Transform]]; sample it and it becomes
the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]]. See [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]].
